5.4.5    Machine Learning Tracking

Why is machine learning experiment tracking vital? Data science processes are generally research-centric work; often, multiple parallel experiments are performed, many of which might not ever make it into production. While working on a machine learning project, getting good results from a single model training run is rare that keeping all your machine learning experiments organized can be a real challenge. Having a process that lets you draw valid conclusions out of various experiments is quite vital, which is where machine learning experiment management becomes a key factor in delivering successful outcomes. Day-to-day effort with machine learning models repeatedly boils down to a sequence of experiments before picking a modeling approach, which combines network topology, training data, and various optimizations or tweaks to the models. Also, enterprise users, like machine learning engineers and data scientists, tend to work alone, which gives the false illusion that keeping track of the experimentation process is not important so long as a final model is delivered. Problems arise when you need to go back to an earlier idea, re-run a model that you may have experimented with only months ago, or simply compare and visualize the differences between runs. With these cases, the need for a system or tool for tracking machine learning experiments is (painfully) apparent. Machine learning tracking allows data scientist teams to see what others are doing; share ideas and insights; and store experiment metadata, which can be retrieved and analyzed at any time. Teamwork can be much more efficient, situations where several people work on the same task can be prevented, and the onboarding of new members can be made much more smooth.

The tracking service on the SAP Data Intelligence platform offers a complete framework for data scientists to configure, capture, organize, reproduce, and visualize machine learning experiments. With provisions for capturing multiple aspects of tracking, data scientists can stipulate what information must be captured as part of the experiment (e.g., model parameters, model metrics, model hyperparameters, etc.) and can later view this information through the Metric Explorer within the machine learning scenario manager. Machine learning tracking on the SAP Data Intelligence platform is primarily driven by the tracking SDK, and the required modules, methods, and scripts can be incorporated into experiments in Jupyter Notebook. But before we discuss experiment tracking in more detail, you must first understand some key entities related to tracking, as shown in Figure 5.11, which we’ll describe next.

Figure 5.11    Model Tracking Entities

Let’s review the key entities you’ll need understand to track your machine learning models, such as the following:

  • Run
    A run is an instance of a machine learning experiment. Each run consists of metrics and parameters from one iteration of the machine learning experiment, along with the associated tags and labels. Metrics are used to measure the performance of your machine learning models. Different metrics are used to evaluate different machine learning models. For example, log loss or average accuracy could be used to evaluate a classification task, whereas mean absolute error or root mean square error (RMSE) could be used to evaluate a model that provides a numeric output.

  • Run collection
    A run collection allows you to logically group a number of runs. You can generate run collections by using the tracking functionality of the SAP Data Intelligence Python SDK. When you log runs using the tracking functionality, you can specify a name for your run collection. If you don’t specify a name, the system creates a default run collection for each source (that is, notebook or pipeline). The name of the default run collection is the same as that of the source. These default run collections are shown in the metrics explorer with the suffix (Default).

  • Visual board
    The visual board is the central place for comparing different runs sourced from one or more run collections and is generated using runs that are called source runs. Data from source runs is shown in tabular format under the Data tab of the visual board.

  • Canvas and charts
    The canvas is the part of the visual board that lets you add charts to compare source runs graphically. For example, to plot a metric against a run ID, parameter, or timestamp, you can create charts from the metrics and parameters of source runs and compare this information visually using the canvas.

Figure 5.12 shows a glimpse of SAP Data Intelligence’s monitoring capabilities. Now that you have a pretty good understanding of the measurement units behind machine learning tracking, let’s learn how you can implement the machine learning tracking capability.

Figure 5.12    SAP Data Intelligence: Monitoring

Getting started with experiment tracking using Jupyter Notebook is simple. The following code snippet will automatically include all the necessary modules required for experiment tracking:

from sapdi import tracking

After the module-importing statement, you’ll use the following code snippets to mark the beginning and the end of the run:

tracking.start_run(run_collection_name='runcollect1')
tracking.end_run()

In this case, start_run() initializes the tracking run under the provided run collection called 'runcollect1' of type string, which basically allows you to group together different runs of your experiment. Furthermore, when the run is initialized via start_run(), the metadata information, such as the Scenario Details, Source Details, Start Time, etc., is automatically recorded.

To log the execution-related metrics, generate list of metrics, or log execution-related parameters, respectively, you can use the following methods:

  • log_metric

  • log_metrics

  • log_parameters

The following code snippet shows you comprehensively how to embed machine learning tracking scripts inside a pipeline:

from sapdi import tracking
run = tracking.start_run()
# tracking.start_run(run_collection_name='rc1') 
# Use this to group different runs under a collection
params = {
'input_size': 784,
'hidden_size': 500,
'num_classes': 10,
'num_epochs': 2,
'batch_size': 100,
'learning_rate': 0.001,
'model_file': 'model.ckpt'
}
tracking.log_parameters(params)
# the experimental code.
for i in range(params.get('num_epochs')):
tracking.log_metric(name='metric_name', value=1)
# more code
tracking.set_tags({
"tag_key": "tag_value",
"tag_key_n": "tag_value_n"
})
tracking.set_labels({
"accuracy": {
"format_string": "percentage"
}})
# more code
tracking.end_run()

Now that we’ve covered machine learning tracking, in the next section, we’ll introduce you to the SAP Data Intelligence modeler and explore its operator-driven capabilities for building graphs for your business processes.

5.4.6    SAP Data Intelligence Modeler and Built-in Operators

Designed on the SAP Data Intelligence pipeline engine, the SAP Data Intelligence modeler delivers a flow-based programming paradigm for data scientists to create data processing pipelines modeled as computation graphs and executed in a containerized environment that runs on Kubernetes. The modeler application helps you model graphs using a graphical interface and achieve the required data ingestion and transformation capabilities. The modeler comes with 250+ built-in operators that can be directly used to build graphs for your business processes or can be used as the basis for a custom operator to design powerful data pipelines. Using the modeler, you can easily design your data processing pipelines using existing graphs or the available operators. As shown in Figure 5.13, on the left side of the application, you can access all the objects you’ll need to interact with to create your pipelines, while the main screen stores the pipelines and allows you to execute and debrief the results.

Inside the modeler, as shown in Figure 5.14, a pipeline or graph is a network of operators connected to each other using typed input ports and output ports for exchanging data. In this context, an operator is a reactive component representing a vertex of a graph and reacts only to events or messages delivered to the operator through its input ports.

Figure 5.13    SAP Data Intelligence Modeler

Figure 5.14    SAP Data Intelligence: Graphs

Since the operator is totally unaware of graph in which it is defined and unfamiliar with the source and target of its incoming and outgoing connections, the operator can only interact with the environment through its output ports. Figure 5.15 shows a sample operator with its input ports and output ports. Each port is associated with a port type, and the tool uses color coding to identify compatible port types.

Figure 5.15    Operators

An operator is associated with a port of any data type, such as string, blob, int64, float64, byte, message stream, and so on. Operators require a certain runtime environment for their execution, and the SAP Data Intelligence Data modeler provides predefined environments for operators. These environments are made available to users as a library of Docker files. When you execute a pipeline (a graph), the tool translates each operator in the graph into a process. The modeler then searches the Docker files for an environment suitable for the operator’s execution and instantiates a Docker image of that environment. This Docker image and the operator process are executed on a Kubernetes cluster. Predefined operators within the SAP Data Intelligence modeler can be classified into various categories, which we’ll describe next.

Converter

A handful of converters are grouped under this category, as shown in Figure 5.16, and these operators support the different types of conversions often required to transform your business data in various ways, for instance, StreamToString, StringToStream, ToBlob, ToStringType, ToSrting, ToNumber, and ToMessage.

Figure 5.16    Converters

Data Quality

This key set of operators, as shown in Figure 5.17, is focused on managing data quality, including masking data, cleansing data, gaining statistical insights, applying data validation rules, and more.

Figure 5.17    Data Quality Operators

Data Workflows

These are dedicated operators for transforming and transferring data; managing workflows including merging, splitting, and triggering workflows: improving data quality using jobs in SAP Data Services; and sending notifications at certain points in the workflow.

Files

As shown in Figure 5.18, file management is easy with this set of file handling operators, including the ability to monitor, read, write, remove, and list files.

Figure 5.18    Files Operators

Hadoop and Spark

Figure 5.19 shows a set of dedicated operators for managing Hadoop jobs, especially for submitting jobs to Hadoop and clusters using the Apache Livy API, a Representational State Transfer (REST) API provided by different cloud providers. Apache Livy is a service that enables easy interaction with a Spark cluster over a REST interface. With Apache Livy, you can easily submit Spark jobs or snippets of Spark code and retrieve results synchronously or asynchronously. In this set, you can also access Spark Context management, all via a simple REST interface or a remote procedure call (RPC) client library.

Figure 5.19    Hadoop and Spark Operators

Machine Learning Predictive Analytics

Since predictive analytics is a common key requirement across various machine learning scenarios, this operator, shown in Figure 5.20, lets you apply the PA Automated Analytics product, which predicts values based on an existing pretrained models.

Figure 5.20    Predictive Analytics Operator

Multiplexer

A multiplexer is a simple operator for mapping the input of any port to all of its output ports. Additional input and output ports can be added as needed. Figure 5.21 shows a quick snapshot of multiplexers.

Figure 5.21    Multiplexers

Processing

This unique set of operators handles common requirements within graphs, like command execution; constant generation; random data generation at certain intervals; inclusion of Go, JavaScript, Python, and R code snippets; and more. Figure 5.22 shows a quick snapshot of processing-related operators.

Figure 5.22    Processing Operators

SAP Integration

As shown in Figure 5.23, this set of operators are focused on data integration, taking care of the sending, receiving, and formatting of data to/from SAP Analytics Cloud and SAP Cloud Platform Integration.

Figure 5.23    SAP Integration Operators

Machine Learning Core Operators

These dedicated operators are only for creating machine learning pipelines and supporting capabilities, such as model training and serving, and integrates with the scenario management features of the platform. Figure 5.24 shows a quick snapshot of processing-related operators.

Figure 5.24    Machine Learning Core Operators

We’d like to focus on a particular core operator called functional services. With SAP Leonardo Machine Learning Foundation now being dissolved into SAP Data Intelligence, Functional Services are longer available separately and instead is included as an operator as part of the pipeline modeler, as shown in Figure 5.25. Currently, the Functional Services operator offers a rather limited set of pretrained image and text processing-oriented functions, including image classification, feature extraction, OCR, similarity scoring, text classifier, and topic detection.

Figure 5.25    Functional Services Operators

SAP Vora

As shown in Figure 5.26, these dedicated operators handle SAP Vora database-related operations, including the reading, ingestion, and loading of data and includes a message decoder.

Figure 5.26    SAP Vora Operators

Structured Data Operators

These operators, shown in Figure 5.27, handle structured data coming from various data sources like Azure SQL DB, DB2, Google BigQuery SQL, Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL, Oracle, Redshift, and SAP IQ databases.

Figure 5.27    Structured Data Operators

Connectivity

This set of operators primarily takes care of connectivity through HTTP requests and providing WAMP record access and includes the ability to consume or send records from Kafka clusters. You can also send emails; replicate tables; configure MQTT-based connectivity; configure connections Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform, or Amazon Web Services (AWS); and more, as shown in Figure 5.28.

Figure 5.28    Connectivity Operators

Tables

This set of operators, shown in Figure 5.29, handles the generation of table messages based on a user-defined schema, the generation of random data, and the decoding of tabular data.

Figure 5.29    Tables Operators

Text Analysis

This unique set of operators, shown in Figure 5.30, handles natural language processing (NLP) for unstructured textual data by using the text analysis capabilities of SAP Vora.

Figure 5.30    Text Analysis Operators

Utilities

As shown in Figure 5.31, these operators deal with the conversion, aggregation, defining scripts, serializing Python data, application logging, and compiling flowgraphs along with many more helpful operators.

Figure 5.31    Utility Operators

Figure 5.32 shows the overall category of operators supported by the SAP Data Intelligence platform.

Figure 5.32    Categories of Operators

5.5    Migrating to SAP Data Intelligence from SAP Data Hub

With the release of SAP Data Intelligence 3.0 and the lack of new functionalities planned for release after SAP Data Hub 2.7, perhaps migrating to SAP Data Intelligence from SAP Data Hub may seem unnecessary. According to SAP, with the release of SAP Data Intelligence 3.0, SAP Data Hub customers will automatically receive SAP Data Intelligence, and no additional migration effort is needed. Existing customers will now have access to all cloud-based machine learning tools as part of support packages without any additional fee or migration effort required. You’ll still be at liberty to select the deployment model of your choice—whether on-premise, in the cloud, or a combination of the two. In addition to SAP Data Hub, SAP Leonardo Machine Learning Foundation has also been dissolved into the SAP Data Intelligence platform since that solution will no longer be available as a standalone service for new subscriptions and can only be consumed via SAP Data Intelligence. As described throughout this chapter, SAP Data Intelligence offers all the integration, orchestration, metadata management, connectivity, and other rich services of SAP Data Hub with the services of SAP Leonardo Machine Learning in the cloud, along with a lot more new features.

In case you still don’t have access to an SAP Data Intelligence tenant and are really eager to get your hands dirty, you can start immediately by signing up for an on-premise trial edition of SAP Data Intelligence 3.0, which is available for Google Cloud Platform, Amazon Web Services (AWS), and Microsoft Azure, through the SAP Cloud Appliance Library, as shown in Figure 5.33.

Figure 5.33    SAP Data Intelligence Trial Edition 3.0

5.6    Summary

Finally, we’ve concluded our chapter on SAP Data Intelligence, SAP’s data science platform that offers a coherent machine learning and data science foundation that can lead your business processes to evolve into an intelligent enterprise. The name SAP Data Intelligence highlights the solution’s focus on intelligent data processing and the operationalization of machine learning processes in enterprise landscapes. This combination allows you to get the most out of your disparate data assets, which can be easily integrated, intelligently refined, and seamlessly used in your business processes. Data scientists can continue to work with the tools they know and love while IT focuses on prototyping machine learning models to put into production and ensures that innovation and machine learning projects can scale and be properly managed. Accelerating the efficient delivery of your intelligent data with innovative data pipelines can enable smart customer experiences. Knowing your data and improving user experiences with metadata management strategies can improve data visibility and enable pervasive data consumption, thus bringing people, processes, and technologies together to drive enterprise-level AI and more importantly gain business insight. A key point of SAP Data Intelligence is providing you with the freedom to choose the deployment model of your choice—whether on-premise, in the cloud, or a combination of the two.

Part II

Building Machine Learning Applications

6    SAP HANA Predictive Analysis Library

and R IntegrationIn this chapter, we’ll dive deeply into the technical aspects the SAP HANA Predictive Analysis Library (SAP HANA PAL) and SAP HANA with R integration. Both SAP HANA PAL and R provide various functions for machine learning and statistical analysis scenarios. This chapter first outlines the installation and prerequisites for SAP HANA PAL and R integration, then discusses in detail how SAP HANA PAL procedures and R functions can be used from native SAP HANA across different machine learning aspects like modeling, prediction, training, validation, and model comparison. This chapter supplements these concepts with several sample codes for a better understanding.

Predictive analysis requires specialized programs to run machine learning algorithms. These programs are optimized for numerical stability and performance. As you’ve seen in Chapter 4, a number different components in SAP HANA provide specialized operations for machine learning and statistical analysis. In this chapter, we’ll focus on two widely used components provided by SAP—the SAP HANA Predictive Analysis Library (SAP HANA PAL) in Section 6.1 and SAP HANA with R integration in Section 6.2—and discuss in detail how to use these solutions in practice.

6.1    SAP HANA Predictive Analysis Library

The SAP HANA Predictive Analysis Library (SAP HANA PAL) provides various machine learning algorithms in the form of SAP HANA PAL procedures. These procedures can be called from SQLScript procedures to build machine learning models in SAP HANA. The underlying SAP HANA PAL functions can also be executed from flowgraphs in the Application Function Modeler (AFM) tool. SAP HANA PAL is mainly designed for data scientists and machine learning experts and provides flexibility for fine-tuning models to make them suitable for specific scenarios. We introduced you to SAP HANA PAL in Chapter 4, Section 4.1.1. In this chapter, we’ll dive more deeply into SAP HANA PAL to see how SAP HANA PAL procedures are used.

6.1.1    Prerequisites and Installation

SAP HANA PAL is part of the Application Function Library (AFL). To utilize SAP HANA PAL, AFL must be installed in SAP HANA, and the script server must be enabled in your SAP HANA instance.

Note

  • Refer to the SAP Note 1898497 to check for compatibility between the AFL revision number and the SAP HANA revision number.

  • Refer to the SAP HANA Server Installation and Upgrade Guide specific to the installed SAP HANA version/revision for installing AFL (http://s-prs.co/501402).

  • Refer to SAP Note 1650957 for enabling the Script Server.

After installing AFL, you can check three views to verify whether SAP HANA PAL procedures have been successfully installed with the following commands:

  • sys.afl_areas

  • sys.afl_packages

  • sys.afl_functions

Use the following SQL code to check these views:

SELECT * FROM "SYS"."AFL_AREAS" WHERE AREA_NAME = 'AFLPAL';
SELECT * FROM "SYS"."AFL_PACKAGES" WHERE AREA_NAME = 'AFLPAL';
SELECT * FROM "SYS"."AFL_FUNCTIONS" WHERE AREA_NAME = 'AFLPAL';

You can also check the SAP HANA PAL procedures installed in the _SYS_AFL schema by filtering for procedure names including “PAL_”, as shown in Figure 6.1.

Figure 6.1    SAP HANA PAL Procedures in the _SYS_AFL Schema

The following roles are required to execute SAP HANA PAL procedures:

  • AFL__SYS_AFL_AFLPAL_EXECUTE

  • AFL__SYS_AFL_AFLPAL_EXECUTE_WITH_GRANT_OPTION

Prior to SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 02, you would need the role AFLPM_CREATOR_ERASER_EXECUTE to create and drop wrapper SAP HANA PAL procedures.

6.1.2    SAP HANA PAL Procedures

SAP HANA has delivered a comprehensive set of efficient machine learning algorithms through SAP HANA PAL procedures. Prior to SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 02, SAP HANA PAL functions were used for the same purpose. These procedures/functions are the building blocks for implementing native machine learning solutions on the SAP HANA platform using SAP HANA PAL. Each SAP HANA PAL procedure or function focuses on a specific task of a machine learning algorithm.

Chapter 3 provides a complete list of supported machine learning algorithms, associated SAP HANA PAL procedures in SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 04, and SAP HANA PAL functions. Note that the category “Statistics” does not mean these algorithms are the only statistical analysis algorithms supported by SAP HANA PAL. These algorithms provide useful statistics for model validation and testing, all grouped under the category “Statistics.” However, many other statistical analysis algorithms are also supported by SAP HANA PAL. In fact, machine learning uses many statistical analysis methods in areas like regression analysis, classification, time series analysis, survival analysis, and data preprocessing; these methods were developed long before machine learning evolved as a subject.

Before we dive more deeply into SAP HANA PAL procedures, let’s recall from Chapter 3 the main steps involved in a typical machine learning project and understand where SAP HANA PAL procedures can be used. As shown in Figure 6.2, except for the steps described in Chapter 3 that deal with the business understanding and process-specific activities like deployment and operationalization, SAP HANA PAL procedures can be used in all major steps in a machine learning project.

Figure 6.2    Major Steps in a Machine Learning Project Where SAP HANA PAL Procedures Can Be Used

Different SAP HANA PAL procedures have been delivered for different machine learning algorithms and different tasks across lifecycle phases. However, some SAP HANA PAL procedures can be used at different phases possibly with different sets of parameters, and some SAP HANA PAL procedures are applicable for only one phase. Figure 6.3 shows an example of SAP HANA PAL procedures across lifecycle phases. Note that the PAL_KNN and PAL_DOUBLE_EXPSMOOTH procedures can be used for both model building and prediction. However, the PAL_DECISION_TREE procedure can be used only for modeling, and the PAL_DECISION_TREE_PREDICT procedure can be used only for prediction. These limitations are mainly due to the inherent nature of the underlying algorithms. In some cases, the way procedures evolved and designed also played a role in their ultimate evolution.

Figure 6.3    Different SAP HANA PAL Functions across Lifecycle Steps

Now, let’s look more closely at procedures. If we open a procedure in SAP HANA, you’ll see a single line of code that passes parameters to a function. That function in turn executes the machine learning algorithm logic. The code shown in Listing 6.1 is from the KNN_CV procedure, which calls the function KNN_CV_ANY.

CREATE PROCEDURE "_SYS_AFL"."PAL_KNN_CV" ( IN p1 table(...), IN p2 table(...), OUT p3 table(...), OUT p4 table(...) ) LANGUAGE AFLLANG SQL SECURITY INVOKER READS SQL DATA AS BEGIN AFLLANGVERSION='2'; SCHEMA='_SYS_AFL'; AREA='AFLPAL'; FUNCTION='KNN_CV_ANY'; PARAMETERS='TREX_TABLE_ANY--;"TABLE",in,TrexTableAny,,,,; 
"TABLE",in,TrexTableAny,,,,;"TABLE",out,TrexTableAny,,,,;"TABLE",out, 
TrexTableAny,,,,;'; END

Listing 6.1    Code of the PAL_KNN_CV Procedure

So, the core machine learning function acts like a black box, but it interacts through the input and output parameters of the procedure. These functions are like database procedures written in C++ to carry out complex data-intensive calculations. These functions are invoked from SAP HANA SQLScript-based SAP HANA PAL procedures. These SAP HANA PAL procedures act like wrapper procedures surrounding these machine learning functions.

Note that a few commonalities exist across SAP HANA PAL procedures, such as the following:

  • All are stored in the _SYS_AFL schema.

  • Their names start with PAL_.

  • They are written in the AFLLANG language.

  • They have some input and output parameters of type TABLE.

Most importantly, the input and output parameters are not static, with predefined table signatures. Instead, input tables of different column structures can be passed through the same parameter as long as you follow certain broad restrictions.

With these initial observations, let’s now understand how these SAP HANA PAL procedures are designed. Figure 6.4 shows a schematic representation of an SAP HANA PAL procedure.

Figure 6.4    Schematic Representation of an SAP HANA PAL Procedure

Each SAP HANA PAL procedure runs a specific task in a machine learning algorithm, like modeling based on some algorithm, evaluating models, or predicting based on a predefined model. All these tasks are based on data, and this data must be supplied to the SAP HANA PAL procedure in input tables. Also, SAP HANA PAL procedures feature various settings and tuning options based on the specific parameters of the underlying algorithms, so these parameter values must also be provided as an input table. Therefore, in almost all SAP HANA PAL procedures, two input tables are required: the data table and the parameter table. Moreover, some procedures require additional input in the form of additional input tables. The results after running the algorithms are provided via output tables. An output table could contain model-specific information (e.g., a coefficient table); fitted data as per the model (e.g., a fitted table); or statistics for model goodness of fit (e.g., statistics table). The output table generation process varies based on:

  • The underlying machine learning algorithm.

  • The parameters specified in the parameter table.

Depending on the parameters specified, the algorithm may execute additional calculations and generate additional output tables.

Data Table

The data table provides the data to be analyzed through machine learning. Depending on the underlying algorithm, this table can have various structures. For regression or classification problems, we’re trying to predict the value of a dependent variable, say Y, based on a set of independent variables, say X1, X2, ... , Xn. Also, to identify the records correctly, we may need an ID column. If this data pertains to a set of customers, then the customer ID may be an identifier for specific records. Thus, in this scenario, the associated algorithm expects data in the structure shown in Table 6.1.

Column Position

Columns

Column Significance

1

ID

The ID column is mandatory for some procedures, like PAL_KNN but not others; if omitted, that value must be specified through a parameter (e.g., parameter HAS_ID in PAL_LINEAR_REGRESSION).

2

Y

The dependent variable of the model.

3 to n

X1, X2, ..., Xn

The independent variables of the model.

Table 6.1    Typical Data Table Structure for Regression- or Classification-Related SAP HANA PAL Procedures

However, for unsupervised learning algorithms, like clustering and association analysis, variables are not easily categorized as either a dependent or an independent variable. Instead, the analysis is performed based on features. Therefore, the associated algorithm expects data in the structure shown in Table 6.2.

Column Position

Columns

Column Significance

1

ID

This column is the identifier of individual records; sometimes, referred to as Customer ID, Document ID, or Transaction ID.

2 ... n

F1, F2, ..., Fn

These columns are the features based on which the clustering or association will be performed. For association analyses, algorithms like apriori, FP-growth, and KORD consider only one feature. Sequential pattern mining considers two features.

Table 6.2    Typical Data Table Structure for Clustering- or Association Analysis-Related SAP HANA PAL Procedures

Note

Consider the following rules while preparing the data table:

  • You’ll need to determine whether the SAP HANA PAL procedure requires an ID column and, if so, what column to use.

  • Some SAP HANA PAL procedures cannot handle NULL or missing values. So, if the data contains NULL, either the associated records must be removed, or these missing values must be imputed.

  • Some SAP HANA PAL procedures require that categorical variables be binarized, either implicitly or explicitly. The following algorithms support implicit binarization through one-hot encoding. For others, your data will need to be prepared through binarization:

    • Accelerated K-means

    • DBSCAN

    • Gaussian mixture model (GMM)

    • Generalized linear models

    • K-means

    • K-medians

    • K-medoids

    • Multiple linear regression

    • Logistic regression (with elastic net regularization)

    • Multi-class logistic regression

    • K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)

    • Multilayer perceptron

    • Support Vector Machine (SVM)

Parameter Table

The machine learning algorithms in SAP HANA PAL support model specification and fine-tuning through parameters. These parameters vary depending on the underlying algorithms. Parameters may be mandatory or optional. The values of these parameters are provided through the parameter table. The parameters have specific names, and their values may be an integer (type INTEGER), a real number (type DOUBLE), or a character (type VARCHAR). The structure of our parameter table is listed in Table 6.3.

Column Name

Data Type

Comments

PARAM_NAME

VARCHAR

Parameter name.

INT_VALUE

INTEGER

Value of the integer type parameters; NULL otherwise.

DOUBLE_VALUE

DOUBLE

Value of the double type parameters; NULL otherwise.

STRING_VALUE

VARCHAR

Value of the string type parameters; NULL otherwise.

Table 6.3    Structure of a Parameter Table

In most of the cases, each parameter requires a single value, but a few parameters may require more than one value be supplied.

For example, let’s consider the SAP HANA PAL procedure PAL_CORRELATION_FUNCTION. This procedure calculates the statistical correlation function between random variables, in the context of time series data. This procedure is also known as an autocorrelation function (ACF). The corresponding parameters of this procedure are listed in Table 6.4.

Parameter Name

Data Type

Possible Values

Default Value

Dependency

THREAD_RATIO

DOUBLE

The ratio of available threads to be used for calculation:

  • 0: single thread

  • 0 to 1: percentage of threads

  • Others: heuristically determined

–1

Required only when a brute force method is used.

USE_LFT

INTEGER

Method to be used:

  • –1: Automatically determined

  • 0: Brute force

  • 1: Fast Fourier Transformation (FFT)

–1

MAX_LAG

INTEGER

Maximum lag for the correlation function

Sqrt (no of records)

CALCULATE_PACF

INTEGER

Calculate PACF?

  • 0: No

  • 1: Yes

1

Only when one series is provided.

Table 6.4    Parameters of PAL_CORRELATION_FUNCTION

Note that all these parameters are optional. If we don’t specify any parameters, the procedure will run with its default values, but you may not get the result you want. Table 6.5 shows an example parameter table.

PARAM_NAME

INT_VALUE

DOUBLE_VALUE

STRING_VALUE

USE_LFT

1

NULL

NULL

MAX_LAG

5

NULL

NULL

Table 6.5    Example of a Parameter Table for PAL_CORRELATION_FUNCTION

In our example, we’re specifying that the fast fourier transformation (FFT) method should be used for calculation, and the maximum lag should be 5. Note that we didn’t specify the value of the CALCULATE_PACF parameter in our case because by default its value is 1 (Yes), and we would like to calculate PACF in our example. Note also that we didn’t specify a value for the THREAD_RATIO parameter because this parameter does not have any effect if the FFT method is used.

To avoid a conflict among the table names when multiple users call SAP HANA PAL procedures simultaneously, we recommended you create the parameter table as a local temporary column table called from the SQL Editor, so that each parameter table has its own scope per session.

Output Table

Output tables are generated by SAP HANA PAL procedures to store the result of the execution of a machine learning algorithm. SAP HANA PAL procedures determine the output table structure without explicit definition, based on the specific rules that apply to the various scenarios:

  • Some output tables have a fixed number of columns, predefined column names, and preassigned data types. All these defaults are predefined by SAP HANA PAL.

  • In some cases, the column name and data type in the output table are inherited from the input data table (e.g., the ID column).

  • In some cases, the entire input table structure is inherited in the output table.

  • Sometimes, the column name is inherited from the input data table with additional suffixes.

  • Sometimes, the column type is widened to the DOUBLE type in the output for a similar column in the input data of the INTEGER type.

SAP HANA PAL procedures provide some flexibility with output tables. They require only matching data types of output columns of the output tables. You can pass tables with different column names but matching data types as output tables to SAP HANA PAL procedures.

Note

Refer to the SAP HANA Predictive Analysis Library (SAP HANA PAL) documentation for complete information on the following topics:

  • Available SAP HANA PAL procedures and underlying machine learning algorithms

  • Required input and output tables for each procedure and their structures

  • List of different parameters associated with each procedure, their usage, and their default values

Specific prerequisites exist for each SAP HANA PAL procedure, like NULL handling, category variable handling, and ID fields.

6.1.3    Calling SAP HANA PAL Procedures

SAP HANA PAL procedures can be called in multiple ways in SAP HANA: from the SQL Editor, from an SQLScript procedure, or from a flowgraph using the AFM tool. The first option is used mainly during model exploration and for checking results. Once a model is finalized, the model can be implemented through a procedure or flowgraph. This section discusses these different options with sample data and code to enhance your understanding. All the codes used in this section are available in text format at this book's website (www.sap-press.com/5014).

Throughout this section, we used the schema ML_DATA as the default schema and the table LM_INPUT_DATA from this schema as the data table. A glimpse of the data is shown in Figure 6.5.

The data has an ID column, an identifier for each observation record. Y is a dependent variable and X1, X2, X3, and X4 are independent variables. All these fields except X4 are numeric, and X4 is a categorical variable (i.e., a factor; it has values “Yes” or “No”). In our scenario, we want to determine whether any relationships exist between Y and the other variables X1, X2, X3, and X4. We’ll start by investigating a linear relationship and then try to fit a multiple linear regression model to the data. The associated SAP HANA PAL procedure is _SYS_AFL.PAL_LINEAR_REGRESSION.

Figure 6.5    Part of the LM_INPUT_DATA Data Table Used in This Section

Also, we’ll use table LM_PARAM, shown in Figure 6.6, as the parameter table for this example.

Figure 6.6    Table LM_PARAM: The Parameter Table Used in This Section

The SAP HANA PAL procedure requires two input tables: the data table and the parameter table. The output is provided through the following five tables:

  • The coefficient table provides the regression model coefficients.

  • The predictive modeling markup language (PMML) table provides the model in PMML format.

  • The fitted table is a table with the fitted values of dependent variable (in our case, Y).

  • The statistics table provides model goodness-of-fit statistics.

  • The optimal parameter table contains the optimal parameter values when specific modeling options and when parameter selection is used. This table, for example, would store the optimal values of model parameters λ and α in an elastic net regression model.

  • Once the model is finalized, you can use the model to predict the values of a dependent variable from observations made on independent variables. We’ll use table LM_NEW_DATA in the ML_DATA schema as our new data table. Figure 6.7 shows the associated data.

Figure 6.7    New Data to Be Used for Prediction Purposes

Note that this data table lacks a column for the dependent variable Y. After all, the value of this variable is what must be predicted.

Let’s now explore the different ways we can run this analysis. The basic idea behind all these different ways is the same: Simply call the SAP HANA PAL procedure with your input tables and get the output tables. Differences only arise in their implementations.

Calling from the SQL Editor

As you explore different models, you don’t always need to store the output. You may not even know if the explored model is the optimal model. In this scenario, you can call an SAP HANA PAL procedure from the SQL Editor. Use the code shown in Figure 6.8 to run a procedure.

Figure 6.8    Sample Code for Running the SAP HANA PAL Procedure from the SQL Editor

Note

  • In this example, we used a local temporary column table as the parameter table. In other words, not even the parameters need to be stored permanently, in a database table.

  • The names of temporary tables start with a hashmark (#).

  • Since output tables are not specified, the output will be displayed on the screen. In our example, we used a question mark (?) in place of the output parameters.

  • The output will show the five tables on the screen; however, the PMML table and the optimal parameter table will display no data since we did not specify any suitable parameter in the parameter table to generate the associated output.

Figure 6.9 shows the output tables associated with the analysis when run from the SAP Web IDE.

Figure 6.9    Output Screen after Running the SAP HANA PAL Procedure from the SQL Editor

These tables are displayed on screen and are not permanently stored. Under the Result1 tab is the coefficient table, showing the coefficients of the independent variables and the intercept term, with associated t-statistics and p-values for their significance. If a p-value is less the 0.05, the influence of the corresponding variable is assumed to be significant, as described in Chapter 2. The model can be interpreted in the following way:

Y = 5.082344440950587 + 3.3682703601715 * X1 + 6.901170525876566 * X2 – 1.9324716286467696 * X3 + 2.949255249095389 * (1 if X4 = ’Yes’; 0 if X4 = ’No’).

The Result3 and Result4 tabs show the fitted values and statistics tables, as shown in Figure 6.10 and Figure 6.11.

Figure 6.10    Output Table with Fitted Value of Y Based on the Regression Equation

Figure 6.11    Output Table with Statistics on Model Fitting

Note that the adjusted R2 value is close to 1. Thus, this model fits the data particularly well. But this model still might not be the best model!

As mentioned earlier, the PMML table and optimal parameter tables lack data since we didn’t instruct the SAP HANA PAL procedure to generate them through the parameter table. So, don’t get confused if you see some empty tables; this scenario may not always be due to an error. The output of PMML table is shown in Figure 6.12.

Figure 6.12    Empty PMML Table

Note the additional table under the Result6 tab, as shown in Figure 6.13, which displays the values of the output parameters (of the SAP HANA PAL procedure) in the SAP Web IDE.

Now, to run the procedure with a specific parameter table and store the result of the output in database tables, use the code shown in Figure 6.14 to call the SAP HANA PAL procedure.

The first time you run this code, comment out the DROP TABLE statements, or you will get errors. (Tables that haven’t been created cannot be dropped.) Then, when you run this code, you’ll create the database tables for containing the output (without any data) and specify these tables in the output parameters of SAP HANA PAL procedure.

Figure 6.13    Extra Table in the SAP Web IDE Showing Values of Output Parameters of the Procedure

Figure 6.14    Code to Call SAP HANA PAL Procedure from the SQL Editor with Saving the Output Tables in the Database

In our example, we used the database table ML__DATA.LM_PARAM as the parameter table, instead of putting these values into a local temporary column table. The code shown in Listing 6.2 can be used to generate this database table.

SET SCHEMA ML_DATA;
CREATE COLUMN TABLE LM_PARAM("PARAM_NAME" VARCHAR(256), "INT_VALUE" INTEGER, 
"DOUBLE_VALUE" DOUBLE,"STRING_VALUE" VARCHAR(1000));
    INSERT INTO "LM_PARAM" VALUES ('STAT_INF',1,NULL,NULL);
    INSERT INTO "LM_PARAM" VALUES ('ADJUSTED_R2',1,NULL,NULL);
    INSERT INTO "LM_PARAM" VALUES ('BP_TEST',1,NULL,NULL);
    INSERT INTO "LM_PARAM" VALUES ('KS_TEST',1,NULL,NULL);

Listing 6.2    Code for Creating the Parameter Table

The data in the five output tables will be exactly the same as before, but this time, this data will be stored in the database tables specified by the table names in the output parameters of the procedure call. You will not see the data on the screen. To view the contents of these database tables, either use the popup menu or use a SELECT statement. The only output you’ll see on the screen is the mapping between the output parameters and the associated tables, as shown in Figure 6.15, which is similar to the table under the Result6 tab in the previous case.

Figure 6.15    Screen Output Showing Output Parameters and Associated Tables

Tip

Don’t get confused with usage of the word “parameter” in different contexts. In general, parameters help define or characterize a system. We used the term “parameter” in this section in two different contexts (hence different underlying systems). A “parameter table” specifies the characteristics of an underlying machine learning function, while “the parameter of a procedure” specifies the input/output of a procedure. The context of the sentence should indicate which sense of “parameter” we’re using.

Calling from SQLScript Procedures

Once a machine learning model is finalized, you should store the associated code somewhere to run it in future. If the model is deployed in production, you cannot run the associated code from the SQL Editor. Thus, SAP has provided the option of calling an SAP HANA PAL procedure from an SQLScript procedure, commonly known as a stored procedure. A stored procedure can be transported to other systems and can be scheduled to run, if required.

The code shown in Figure 6.16 is an example of how to use an SQLScript procedure to call an SAP HANA PAL procedure.

Figure 6.16    Sample Code for Calling the SAP HANA PAL Procedure from an SQLScript Procedure

Note

The code creates a procedure called PROC_REGRESSION MODEL in the ML_DATA schema. This procedure calls the SAP HANA PAL procedure. The input data table and parameter table are already available and are passed to the SAP HANA PAL procedure as table variables. Input tables cannot be passed directly to an SAP HANA PAL procedure in a nested call.

The output table parameters passed to the SAP HANA PAL procedure become table variables inside the procedure. These table variables are then used to store data into output tables. The output tables are already created with the specified structure. You can reuse part of the code shown earlier in Figure 6.14, the part that creates the output tables.

Before storing the data into these output tables, the output tables are truncated to delete any data from earlier runs of the code.

A colon (:) is used before a name to indicate that it is a variable.

In our example, we did not specify the Security clause in the procedure definition. You may put “Definer” or “Invoker” in the procedure definition based on your security requirements.

Once defined, you can run the SAP HANA PAL procedure with the following statement:

Call ML_DATA.PROC_REGRESSION_MODEL();

This statement will run the procedure, and the output will be stored in the specified tables. This time, no additional table, like the table shown earlier in Figure 6.15, is created. As expected, the five output tables will contain exactly the same data when run from the SQL Editor.

Now, once you’ve finalized the model, you can use the model to make predictions. However, SAP HANA PAL provides a separate procedure (_SYS_AFL.PAL_LINEAR_REGRESSION_PREDICT) for predictions using linear regression models, which involve a different structure for the data table and for the parameter table. We’ll use the table shown earlier in Figure 6.7 as the data table but use table LM_PARAM_PREDICTION, shown in Figure 6.17, as the parameter table.

Figure 6.17    Parameter Table for Prediction

This SAP HANA PAL procedure requires another input table: the coefficient table, with only the variable name. Coefficient values are obtained from the finalized model. Our prediction will be based on the fitted model, and the coefficients from the final model captures this information.

The procedure shown in Figure 6.18 can be used to run the prediction.

Figure 6.18    Procedure for Prediction Based on Selected Regression Model

Note

  • The input parameters for coefficients are selected from the coefficient table of the final model.

  • The output table contains the ID column and the predicted values of the variable Y.

  • The parameter table we used in our case is specific to this procedure; do not confuse it with the earlier parameter table we used for modeling.

Figure 6.19 shows the data in the output table LM_PREDICTED_VAL.

Figure 6.19    Predicted Values of Y Using the New Dataset

Calling SAP HANA PAL Functions Using Flowgraphs

The various SAP HANA PAL functions for different machine learning algorithms can be called from flowgraphs in the AFM tool. Flowgraphs allow you to create a data flow network with individual nodes for specific tasks, linked together to form the entire flow. A specific machine learning function can be added as a node in a flowgraph from the Predicted Analysis Library component of the Palette. The signatures of the input tables, signatures of the output tables, and the parameter values for the SAP HANA PAL function can be specified through the properties of their respective anchors on the node. The input and output tables can be specified through the Data Source and Data Sink (Template Table) nodes of the Palette, respectively. The link between the input tables to the SAP HANA PAL function and the link between the SAP HANA PAL function to the output tables can be achieved by holding the connect button of the respective source node and dragging and dropping the vector onto the target node. Once the flowgraph is saved and activated, you can execute the flowgraph by clicking the Execute button and choosing one of the following three options: Execute in SQL Editor, Open in SQL Editor, or Execute and Explore. The SAP HANA PAL function will be executed with the input data and will provide the output in the specified data sink template tables.

6.1.4    Model Evaluation

Machine learning models are evaluated primarily based on two approaches: checking the goodness-of-fit statistics and validating the fitted model using a validation dataset (if training is applicable). This second approach is known as model validation, which we discussed in detail in Chapter 3. In this section, we’ll focus on how you can implement model validation concepts in SAP HANA PAL.

Some machine learning algorithms use tuning or penalty parameters during the model fitting process, and different values for these parameters result in different models. For example, in a ridge regression algorithm and a lasso algorithm, different values for the penalty parameter (λ) produces different models. Thus, selecting the optimal value of this penalty parameter is important, and the process of determining this optimal value is known as optimal parameter selection.

SAP HANA PAL supports model validation and optimal parameter selection for the following SAP HANA PAL procedures:

  • PAL_FRM

  • PAL_ALS

  • PAL_LINEAR_REGRESSION

  • PAL_POLYNOMIAL_REGRESSION

  • PAL_LOGISTIC_REGRESSION

  • PAL_MULTILAYER_PERCEPTRON

  • PAL_NAIVE_BAYES

  • PAL_DECISION_TREE

  • PAL_SVM

  • PAL_KNN_CV

Important Note

Model validation using training and validation datasets is applicable for supervised learning, where the model can be trained based on historical data. However, for unsupervised learning, machine learning algorithms identify patterns from the data, and no concept of training exists. Thus, the concepts involving validation datasets discussed in this section are only applicable for supervised learning algorithms. Furthermore, within supervised learning, no notion of training exists in the k-nearest neighbors algorithm, and thus, for this algorithm, SAP HANA PAL includes a separate procedure for validation: the PAL_KNN_CV procedure.

Model Validation

SAP HANA PAL provides various model fitting statistics based on the parameters selected. These statistics can be used to validate the fitted model. SAP HANA PAL also supports k-fold cross validation and the Bootstrap method for creating the training and validation datasets from the original data table. For classification problems (where the response variable, i.e., the dependent variable is categorical), SAP HANA PAL provides a stratified version of these methods, and data is sampled proportionately from each category. This option is specified by the mandatory parameter RESAMPLING_METHOD in the parameter table. Table 6.6 shows the parameters associated with the resampling technique.

Parameter Name

Data Type

Values

Default Value

Comment

RESAMPLING_METHOD

NVARCHAR

 
cv
stratified_cv
bootstrap
stratified_bootstrap

None

Mandatory parameter.

The value cv implies k-fold sampling. Both cv and bootstrap have stratified versions.

EVALUATION_METRIC

NVARCHAR

 
ACCURACY
ERROR_RATE
F1_SCORE
RMSE
MAE
AUC
NLL

None

Mandatory parameter. The values are the different measures based on which validation is performed.

FOLD_NUM

INTEGER

Number of folds (k) for a k-fold cross-validation.

None

Optional parameter.

REPEAT_TIMES

INTEGER

Number of times validations to be carried out.

1

Table 6.6    Parameters for Model Validation

When validation parameters are specified, SAP HANA PAL provides additional statistics in the statistics table to represent the model’s goodness of fit based on the validation dataset. In the next section, we’ll provide an example covering both optimal parameter selection and validation.

Optimal Parameter Selection

For selecting the optimal value of the tuning or penalty parameters, SAP HANA PAL procedures run the model fitting with a set of different values of these parameters. These different values may come from a grid (i.e., a predefined set of values) or chosen randomly within a range. Different models thus fitted with different values of the parameter are then compared with respect to some metrics like accuracy, error rate, root mean squared error (RMSE), and AUC on the validation dataset, and the parameter values associated with the optimal model is reported.

Important Note

The optimal parameter selection for supervised learning models works on the validation dataset. Different models usually tend to fit well with the training dataset, so their performance can be judged properly with validation data that is not used for training. Depending on the performance of different model tuning parameters on validation data, the best tuning or penalty parameters are selected. You’ll still need to run validation for the optimal parameter selection.

Like model validation, the optimal parameter selection is specified through parameters in the parameter table. The parameters listed in Table 6.7 are available for this purpose.

Parameter Name

Data Type

Values

Default Value

Comment

PARAM_SEARCH_STRATEGY

NVARCHAR

  • grid

  • random

Specifies how the parameter values will be selected.

None

Optional parameter.

RANDOM_SEARCH_TIMES

INTEGER

Number of times parameter values to be selected randomly.

None

Optional parameter, but mandatory and valid when parameter values are selected randomly.

SEED

INTEGER

Specifies the seed for random number selection.

0

Optional parameter. Used when parameter values are selected randomly.

Table 6.7    Parameters for Optimal Parameter Selection

Note that the parameter EVALUATION_METRIC is also used for optimal parameter selection. The measure specified in this parameter is used to find the optimal tuning parameter.

Some other parameters, applicable for both validation and parameter selection, are listed in Table 6.8.
